identity.author: John Davenant
identity.work: Two Dissertations (De praedestinatione through Cap. X Arg. VI+)
identity.edition: Dissertationes duae (Cambridge: Roger Daniel, 1650). Partial through Cap. X Arg. VI Principatus + Arg. VII Arminius open. Further Cap. X remains.

scope.locus: De praedestinatione Cap. X Arg. V Minor close + Arg. VI Principatus + Arg. VII Arminius open.
scope.next_locus: Cap. X Arg. VII cont. (Isa. liii.10 / Augustine De praedest. sanct. 10 — promise of church; then infants Arg.).

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. V Minor cont.: Tract. 107 — the Father’s prior giving makes them not of the world Christ does not pray for; election makes faithful, not faith elect
english: And Tractate 107: By this—that the Father has already given them to him—it comes about that they do not belong to that world for which Christ does not pray. As if to say: antecedent election made them faithful; antecedent faith did not make them elect.
sections.latin: Et Tract. 107. Per hoc quod eos illi Pater jam dedit, factum est ut non pertineant ad eum mundum pro quo non rogat Christus. Quasi dixisset, Per antecedaneam electionem factum est ut essent fideles, non per antecedaneam fidem ut essent electi.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. V Minor: John x. 26 and 1 John ii. 19 — not believing / falling away is posterior to not being Christ’s sheep or of us; Arminius must say non-elect precedes unbeliever
english: Now weigh the Minor’s other part: not believing, or springing back from faith once begun, comes after this divine not-giving—non-election in Christ—and so non-election or reprobation does not arise from such foresight as from an antecedent motive. On unbelief the witness already cited is plain (John x. 26): You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. On apostasy from faith once received, 1 John ii. 19 is clear enough: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. Let Arminius or Corvinus show what not being of Christ’s sheep means, if not not being of the elect. If that is true, then in our order of thought not being elect comes before being an unbeliever.
sections.latin: Jam et alteram partem Minoris pensitemus, nimirum, Quod non-credere, vel a fide incepta resilire sit posterius hac non-datione Divina, sive non-electione in Christo, et per consequens quod non-electio sive reprobatio ex tali praevisione tanquam ex antecedaneo motivo minime oriatur. De Infidelitate valde perspicuum est illud, quod antea citavimus testimonium, Joann. x. 26. Non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus meis. Sic etiam de Apostasia a fide suscepta satis clarum est illud, 1 Joann. ii. 19. E nobis exierunt, sed ex nobis non fuerunt: nam si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utique nobiscum, &c. Ostendat nobis Arminius, aut Corvinus quid sit non esse ex ovibus Christi, nisi non esse ex electis: quod si verum sit, tum non esse electum est quiddam prius consideratione nostra quam esse incredulum.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. V Minor close: apostates were never given to Christ; Augustine De corr. & grat. 7 — non-perseverance follows non-election, not foresight of non-perseverance
english: Explain also that by which apostates, even while with us, are still not of us. They will find nothing to rest in except this: they were not given to Christ by the Father—passed by, reprobated, and not written in the book of life, the catalogue of divine election. So being reprobate or non-elect is prior in order to being foreseen as one who will fall into apostasy and stay there. Augustine saw this rightly (De correptione et gratia 7): Those who will not persevere are not set apart by God’s foreknowledge and predestination from that mass of perdition, and so are neither called according to purpose, nor elect. He does not say they were not elect because they were foreseen as non-persevering; he teaches that those will not persevere who were not antecedently elect and set apart from the mass of perdition.
sections.latin: Expediat etiam quid illud sit per quod apostatae etiam cum nobiscum sunt, non sunt tamen ex nobis. Nihil profecto aliud reperient in quo consistere possunt, praeterquam quod non fuerunt donati Christo a Patre, hoc est praeteriti, reprobati fuerunt, et in libro vitae, sive catalogo electionis Divinae, minime conscripti. Esse ergo reprobatum vel non-electum est ordine prius quam esse praevisum ut in apostasiam labentem et in eadem permanentem. Hoc recte observavit Augustinus, De corr. et grat. cap. 7. hisce verbis, Qui perseveraturi non sunt, non sunt a massa illa perditionis praescientia Dei et praedestinatione discreti, et ideo nec secundum propositum vocati, ac per hoc nec electi. Non dicit Augustinus, quia praevidebantur minime perseveraturi, ideo non fuisse electos: sed docet, eos non esse perseveraturos qui non fuerunt antecedenter electi et a massa perditionis discreti.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. V close / Arg. VI open (Quinto): decree not to give faith is not productive cause of unbelief; Bradwardine — principate over futures and non-futures
english: But lest anyone twist what was said—that not giving to Christ, or not electing, is prior on God’s reprobating side to absolute foresight of not-believing or not-persevering on the reprobate’s side—I warn: this does not mean God or his decree is the productive cause of human unbelief, apostasy, or stubbornness (those spring from inbred corruption). It means that since faith and perseverance are gifts of the merciful God, which he could give to all, by the very act of reprobating he decrees not to work in some what he will work in others and could have worked in all. For as Augustine truly says (De correptione et gratia 24), no human will resists God when he wills to save. So that very resisting—or persevering in unbelief—foreseen in all the reprobate plainly proves that he who holds most omnipotent power to incline human hearts wherever he pleases did not have this efficacious will to save these; which is nothing other than not electing them, or reprobating them. Fifth, the argument is from that principate due to God not only over future things but also over non-future things. For as Bradwardine rightly holds (lib. 3, c. 33), God holds principate not only over beings but also over non-beings.
sections.latin: Sed ne quis inde errandi occasionem arripiat quod dictum est, non-dare Christo vel non-eligere esse prius considerandum ex parte Dei reprobantis, quam non-credere aut non-perseverare absolute praevideatur ex parte personae reprobatae; id moneo non esse ita intelligendum, quasi Deus, aut Dei decretum, causa productiva esset infidelitatis, apostasiae, aut pertinaciae humanae, (haec enim omnia nascuntur ex insita hominum corruptione) sed quia cum fides et perseverantia sint dona Dei miserentis, quae omnibus posset impertire, ipso actu reprobandi decernat apud se non efficere in aliquibus, quod in aliis effecturus est, quodque in omnibus efficere potuisset. Nam (ut vere Augustinus, De corr. et grat. cap. 24.) Deo volenti salvum facere nullum hominum resistit arbitrium. Ipsum itaque resistere, sive in infidelitate perseverare, quod praevidetur in omnibus reprobates, aperte evincit illum qui habet humanorum cordium quocunque placuerit inclinandorum omnipotentissimam potestatem, ut inquit Augustinus ibidem, non habuisse hanc efficacem hosce salvandi voluntatem: quod nil aliud est quam eos non-elegisse sive reprobasse. Quinto arguitur ab illo principatu qui Deo tribuendus est, non modo circa res futuras, sed etiam circa res non futuras. Nam (ut recte statuit Bradwardinus, lib. 3. c. 33.) Deus non solum super entia, sed etiam super non-entia tenet principatum.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. VI: principate forces the issue — non-futurity of faith in some cannot rest on bare foresight; will decrees efficacious operation or its denial
english: That granted: since it is certain and defined for God from eternity that in some men neither repentance nor faith nor perseverance will ever come to be, where do we lodge the principate over these non-futures in the divine will? We cannot say God’s eternal will or some divine decree effects or begets unbelief, impenitence, and apostasy in those men—for God is not author of what he avenges. Nor is it enough to say he foresaw from eternity that such men, given sufficient grace to repent, believe, and persevere, would by their own malice prove impenitent, unbelieving, or apostate. That gives God infallible foresight of futures and non-futures, but still leaves the human will the principal determination of whether those things will exist or not.
sections.latin: Hoc posito, cum ab aeterno certum Deo sit et definitum, quod in quibusdam hominibus nec poenitentia, nec fides, nec perseverantia unquam sit futura, quaeso quorsum reducemus harum rerum non futurarum principatum ad Divinam voluntatem? Non possumus affirmare aeternam Dei voluntatem, aut decretum aliquod Divinum, in istis hominibus efficere sive gignere infidelitatem, impoenitentiam et apostasiam: Deus enim autor non est ejus rei cujus est ultor. Neque sufficit dicere, Deum ab aeterno praevidisse, quod tales homines, administrata illis gratia sufficienti ad poenitendum, credendum et perseverandum, propria sua malitia exsisterent impoenitentes, infideles aut apostatae. Nam hoc Deo quidem tribuit rerum futurarum aut non futurarum praescientiam infallibilem, sed interim humanae voluntati adscribit de futura earundem existentia aut non-futura determinationem principalem.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. VI: therefore God’s will predominates — Cain/Judas/Hymenaeus vs Peter/Paul; reprobation’s non-gift of faith precedes foreseen unbelief
english: So we must come back to this: with God lies the principal determination of futures and non-futures—in good acts, by decreeing to apply his efficacious operation to produce them; in evils produced by the wicked, by decreeing not to hinder them; and in good acts those same would omit, by decreeing not to give the efficacious grace by which they would be done. Thus God’s will is the predominating, predetermining cause of the non-being of things that will not be: he can make them future if he wills, yet he does not will to do what he could. Not willing from eternity—though he could—that Cain repent, Judas believe, Hymenaeus persevere, firmly demonstrates antecedent non-election; willing to bring about that Peter repent, Paul believe and persevere, clearly proves antecedent election. And this reprobation decree—the determined act of the divine will not to give faith, repentance, perseverance to certain persons—must precede their unbelief and impenitence, foreseen and certainly future.
sections.latin: Eo igitur tandem redeundum est, ut fateamur penes Deum esse principalem rerum futurarum et non-futurarum determinationem; quatenus in bonis actibus decrevit ad eos producendos efficacem suam operationem adhibere; quatenus in malis, quae ab hominibus improbis producuntur, decrevit eos minime impedire; denique, quatenus in bonis actibus, qui ab iisdem omitterentur, decrevit non dare gratiam efficacem qua fierent. Et sic voluntas Dei est causa predominans et praedeterminans quoad non-esse rerum minime futurarum, quoniam cum possit facere ut essent futurae si vellet, non vult tamen hoc facere quod posset. Jam vero ab aeterno non velle facere cum posset, ut Cain poeniteat, ut Judas credat, ut Hymenaeus perseveret, est antecedaneae non-electionis firma demonstratio; sicut velle efficere ut Petrus poeniteat, ut Paulus credat et perseveret, est antecedaneae electionis clara probatio. Hoc autem reprobationis decretum, quod continet determinatum actum Divinae voluntatis de non danda fide, poenitentia, perseverantia certis quibusdam personis, earundem infidelitatem, impoenitentiam et praevisam et certo futuram praecedat est necesse.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. VI close: unbelief foreseen in negation of efficacious grace; Augustine De praedest. sanct. 6 — preparing / not preparing the will precedes foresight of faith or unbelief
english: So reprobation is not to be set from foresight of antecedent unbelief, nor election from foresight of faith. Final unbelief in the reprobate is foreseen in the antecedent denial of efficacious grace; persevering faith in the elect is foreseen in the antecedent preparation of that grace—so that on both sides principate, authority, superiority, and determining power over futures and non-futures rest with God as supreme arbiter. That is what Augustine taught (De praedestinatione sanctorum 6): Some believe; others contradict. These will to believe; those will not. Who does not know this? Who denies it? But since the Lord prepares the will for some and not for others, and so on. So the decree to prepare or not prepare human wills is prior to foresight of human faith or unbelief—which is as much as to say that predestination and preterition of singular persons is prior to absolute foreknowledge of faith or unbelief in them.
sections.latin: Non ergo reprobatio ponenda est ex praevisione antecedaneae infidelitatis, nec electio ex praevisione fidei; sed infidelitas reprobatorum finalis praevidetur in antecedente negatione gratiae efficacis, et fides electorum perseverans praevidetur in antecedente praeparatione gratiae efficacis: ut utrobique principatus, authoritas, superioritas et determinativa potestas sive rerum futurarum sive non-futurarum sit penes Deum tanquam supremum arbitrum. Hoc illud est quod docuit Augustinus, de praedest. sanct. cap. 6. Alii credunt, alii contradictunt. Volunt ergo isti credere; nolunt autem illi. Quis hoc ignoret? quis hoc neget? Sed cum aliis praeparetur, aliis non praeparetur voluntas a Domino, &c. Unde patet decretum de praeparandis et non praeparandis humanis voluntatibus esse praevisa sive fide sive infidelitate humana prius: Quod perinde est ac si diceremus, praedestinationem et praeteritionem singularium personarum esse absoluta praescientia fidei aut infidelitatis in eisdem priorem.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. VII open: Arminius’s three decrees leave church-acquisition to free will; Grevinchovius and Episcopius admit redemption may apply to none / church may wholly fail
english: If, as Arminius sets it, after God’s decree to give Christ as Mediator and Savior, and the second decree to save any under the condition of repentance, faith, and perseverance, and the third to administer to all the means needed for repentance and faith—if, with those three decrees in place, election and reprobation of singular persons, salvation and damnation, hang on foresight of men’s faith or unbelief—then it follows that free will was left able to empty out the end of the Lord’s passion, the acquiring of the Church. So that Christ not dying in vain, and having a church of elect efficaciously redeemed by his blood, would come not from some antecedent decree or special grace of God electing certain members to Christ the Head and predestining them to be made alive and saved through him, but from the contingent working of human wills. For all mortals, if taken as not yet elect and not predetermined by that special providence we call Predestination to have faith and persevere in it, can stay in unbelief, spring back from faith once received, in a word fall from salvation and leave Christ the Redeemer with no redeemed church at all. Those who fetch election and reprobation from foresight of faith and unbelief cannot deny this consequence. Grevinchovius admitted it candidly (Dissert. De morte Christi, p. 14): We assert that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none because of the intervening unbelief of all. So Episcopius, resting on this Arminian principle, confesses the whole church on earth can fail, and that Christ need not always have some true church on earth in order to remain King and Head.
sections.latin: Si, ut ponit Arminius, post decretum Dei de dando Christo Mediatore et Salvatore, et illud alterum quo decrevit quosvis sub conditione resipiscentiae, fidei et perseverantiae salvos facere, itemque et illud tertium quo decrevit media ad resipiscentiam et fidem necessaria omnibus administrare; si, inquam, positis hisce tribus decretis, singularium personarum electio et reprobatio, salus et damnatio dependeat ex praevisa hominum sive fide sive infidelitate, tum sequitur, hominum libero arbitrio relictum fuisse, ut possent finem Dominicae passionis, hoc est, acquisitionem Ecclesiae, prorsus evacuare: Ita ut, quod Christus frustra mortuus non fuerit, quod habeat Ecclesiam electorum sanguine suo efficaciter redemptam, non ex antecedaneo aliquo decreto, aut speciali gratia Dei membra quaedam Christo Capiti eligentis et per Christum vivificanda et salvanda praedestinantis, sed ex contingente operatione humanarum voluntatum evenerit. Universi enim mortales, si considerentur ut nondum electi, nec speciali illa providentia Dei, quam Praedestinationem vocamus, ad habendam fidem et perseverandum in eadem praedeterminati, possunt in sua incredulitate manere, possunt a fide suscepta resilire, possunt, uno verbo, a salute excidere, et Christum Redemptorem, absque Ecclesia redempta prorsus relinquere. Hanc consequentiam non possunt negare, qui electionem et reprobationem ex praevisione fidei et infidelitatis conantur arcessere. Ingenue itaque illam admisit Grevinchovius, Dissert. De morte Christi, pag. 14. Asserimus, inquit, potuisse omnibus impetratam esse redemptionem, et tamen nullis applicatam propter intervenientem omnium infidelitatem. Sic etiam Episcopius hoc principio Arminiano innixus, fatetur totam Ecclesiam in terris deficere posse, neque necesse esse ad hoc, ut Christus Rex et Caput maneat, illum habere semper Ecclesiam aliquam veram in terris.
